current_example.title: Example: Sketching the Second Derivative of a Function

q-20255.name: Question 1
q-20255.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190876/assets/d2b5a3500e8e3adf2023a1bfb7fabcd27398b029b87f474d00ffb7ac76b90e2a.png)

The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown above. Which of the following could be the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$, the derivative of $f(x)?$
q-20255.worked_solution:
Notice the following:

- At the stationary points, where the tangent line to $y=f(x)$ is parallel to the $x$-axis, we have ${f}^{′}(x)=0.$

- When $f(x)$ is increasing, we have ${f}^{′}(x)>0.$

- When $f(x)$ is decreasing, we have ${f}^{′}(x)<0.$

We can now summarize the information from the graph in the table below. Note that the stationary point was identified (approximately) from the graph of $y=f(x)$:

| $x$ | $(-\infty ,2.5)$ | $2.5$ | $(2.5,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f$ | $↘$ | $\text{min}$ | $↗$ |
| ${f}^{′}$ | $-$ | $0$ | $+$ |

Additionally, from the graph of $y=f(x),$ we can conclude that there are no inflection points.  Also, the graph of $y=f(x)$ is concave up in $(-\infty ,\infty ).$ So, ${f}^{″}(x)>0$ and $y={f}^{′}(x)$ is increasing.

Therefore, the graph of $y={f}^{′}(x)$ may look as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14190876/assets/fde284c6bda2a0a9dba79a41348cf25ce7d5e5db8d2af996c577ceca721d5ab2.png)
